dup_ex_title: Alkylphenols in human milk and their relations to dietary habits in central Taiwan.
sq_summary: the generator added a month to all 100 year-only requests, so its filter dropped the right paper for 93 of them; checking each extracted value against the request fixed that (found within 1,024 tokens, year-only requests: 22 with no filter, 17 raw filter, 25 checked)
sq_reading: What the numbers say. The generator always produced parseable JSON (300 of 300) and resolved titles well (the right paper alone for 88 of 100 title requests). But it invented values: every one of the 100 year-only requests came back with a month as well (always 12, December), which the request never stated, so the raw filter kept the right paper for only 7 of them and found less than no filter at all (17 against 22). Dropping any extracted value that the request does not literally state (a schema check, no model) keeps the right paper for 100 of 100 and lifts the month-and-year requests from 22 to 32 found. For title requests a filter adds little (34 without, 34 with): the title words in the query already pull the embedding to the right paper. The oracle row (the right paper as the filter) shows how much a correct filter is worth when the request only gives a date: 45 and 60 found.
sb_reading: Step-back hurt every retriever: alone it scores 0.669 (Qwen3), 0.669 (bge-small) and 0.619 (BM25) against 0.700, 0.713 and 0.679 for the claim, and fused with the claim it still loses (0.678, 0.697, 0.652). The general question retrieves general abstracts, and a SciFact claim needs the one specific study. Step-back is designed for questions that need background principles (the paper tested STEM, time-sensitive knowledge and multi-hop questions), not for specific claims.
dec_reading: The 1.7 B generator mostly returned the question unchanged (1.12 sub-questions per question on average), and where it did split, fusing the lists hurt: with bge-small, questions with both gold paragraphs in the top 5 fell from 98 to 85 (bridge) and from 39 to 29 (comparison); BM25 fell the same way.
pa_budget_reading: Strictly right answers barely move with k: 97 of 188 with only the top abstract, 96 at k 3, 96 at k 5 and 101 at k 10, while the prompt grows from 504 to 3,644 tokens on average. The reranked top 3 already holds the evidence for 178 of the 188 claims (root lab), so more abstracts add little to find; this 1.7 B model's limit is reading, not finding (it never answered CONTRADICT in any of these runs, the same failure the root lab found).
pa_pos_summary: gold abstract first, middle or last among 10: 116, 68 and 78 of 188 strictly right (the right label alone: 118, 109, 113)
pa_pos_reading: Position matters a lot here, but not as a U: the evidence first gives 111 (k 5) and 116 (k 10) strictly right of 188; in the middle 71 and 68; last 65 and 78. Look at what changes, though: the right label barely moves (107 to 118 of 188 across all six placements), the citation does. With the evidence elsewhere, the model still cites abstract [1] in 59 of 188 answers at k 10 (gold in the middle) and 45 (gold last), a pull toward the first abstract shown. So for this model, put the best chunk first, and treat citations to the first position with suspicion.
pa_cite_reading: All three formats could be parsed and resolved to an abstract in the prompt for every answer (188, 188, 188 of 188), so labels the model can copy are what matters, not their style; corpus ids did as well as numbers (99 against 96 strictly right). Asking for a quote changed the answers themselves: the model never answered NOT ENOUGH INFO (0 times, against 25 with numbers), which raised strictly right answers to 108, but only 71 of its 188 quotes were found word for word in the cited abstract; the rest paraphrased or quoted the claim back. Strictly right with a verified quote: 38.
late_summary: hurt here: paragraph-aware chunks found within 1,024 tokens 0.733 → 0.684, fixed windows 0.556 → 0.536 (modernbert-embed-base)
late_detail: it did not help. Within each question's own paper, at a 1,024-token budget, paragraph-aware chunks found 0.733 of questions embedded one by one and 0.684 with late chunking; fixed 256-token windows 0.556 against 0.536; the top-1 chunk is right for 0.318 against 0.243 (paragraph-aware) measured. The setting explains it: every chunk competing here comes from the same paper, so the document-wide context late chunking adds is shared by all of them and makes them more alike, not easier to tell apart. The published gains come from search across many documents (BEIR), where knowing which document a chunk belongs to is exactly what separates it. Cost: one pass over each whole paper (19 of 281 papers were longer than 8,192 tokens and went through in overlapping windows) took 376 s against 168 s for embedding the chunks one by one on MPS, because attention over long sequences costs more than over many short ones. The root lab's contextual prefixes showed the same within-paper pattern.
sparse_detail: opensearch-neural-sparse-encoding-doc-v3-distill (67 M parameters, Apache 2.0) through sentence-transformers' SparseEncoder, documents encoded on MPS (42 and 38 documents per second, load average about 11 to 18 from other jobs). nDCG@10: SciFact 0.708 against 0.679 for BM25 and 0.700 for Qwen3-Embedding; NFCorpus 0.345 against 0.318 and 0.363 measured. Fused with Qwen3-Embedding by RRF it scores 0.724 (SciFact) and 0.364 (NFCorpus), level with BM25 + Qwen3 (0.724, 0.361). A document keeps 239 non-zero terms on average and a query 20 (SciFact) or 5 (NFCorpus), so the index stays an inverted index. Caveat: the model card lists SciFact and NFCorpus among its training sets, so these scores are in-domain and flatter it against BM25 and the dense models, which never saw these sets.
